newsitem.title: USA: NY gold, silver end sharply lower, palladium up.
newsitem.headline: NY gold, silver end sharply lower, palladium up.

text.p: COMEX gold and silver futures ended sharply lower Tuesday, but platinum group metals (PGM) futures held up well with new contract highs in platinum and palladium ended up by the daily limit for the third straight day.
"We think gold is going lower," Chicago Corp's COMEX floor trader Carlos Perez-Santalla said.
"U.S. gold mining companies have cheaper leaching processes now at less than $200 an ounce which give them a lot more money in their forward sales and we expect a lot more of them," he said.
"The health of the equity and bond markets, the lack of any visible inflation, and the strength of the dollar - you name it, there isn't anything that points higher for gold," he said.
The U.S. dollar climbed to new seven year highs against the deutschmark Tuesday and new seven year highs on its trade weighted index.
COMEX December gold ended down $3.50 an ounce at $324.60, after seeing a three week low intraday at $321.00 an ounce.
COMEX gold estimated volume was moderate at 42,000 lots.
Minor support around $326.00 broke down in COMEX December gold, triggering stop loss execution below $326.00 and below $324.00, traders said.
Daily momentum oscillators are also now weakening again, suggesting the shortcovering rally of the past three weeks may be coming to an end, analysts said.
COMEX gold open interest rose 1,435 lots Monday to 188,024 contracts, suggesting funds may be re-establishing short positions, after several weeks of profit taking and short covering.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $320.20/70, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $321.10 and the New York close Monday at $323.65/15.

COMEX silver was even weaker than gold, with the active September contract ending down 19.2 cents at $4.315 an ounce, after breaking back below a recent uptrend line at $4.50, and then breaking more significant support at $4.40, traders said.

COMEX warehouse silver stocks also rose 607,502 ounces Monday to 169,686,183 ounces, after falling steadily in recent weeks to their lowest level Friday since the addition of Wilmington Trust stocks in January.

"I see no fundamental justification for the recent rally in silver, and we failed at resistance near the 40-day moving average today, and then the key support around $4.40 failed also," Merrill Lynch's commodity research director, Bill O'Neill said.
NYMEX October platinum ended down $5.60 an ounce at $449.60, but not before setting a new contract high early at $466.00, and then swinging through a wide $26.50 intraday range.
The October NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread ended at a $127.50, just below Monday's new high at $129.50.
But NYMEX September palladium ended up the $12.00 limit for the day at a new contract high at $227.60 an ounce, after spot palladium fixed at a fresh 17 year high at $245.50 in London Tuesday.
Earlier TOCOM palladium futures went limit up for the fifth straight session in Tokyo overnight.

No further Russian shipments of platinum group metals (PGMs) are expected in Japan under the annual supply contract until around August 10, and offerings by Russia in the spot market are not meeting pent up demand, traders said.
"The underlying rate of demand growth for palladium is running at double digit figures," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a report.
"Up until recently it was generally assumed by most observers, including ourselves, that the Russians would go on meeting this demand increase from mine production and stockpile material," he said.
"Now we are beginning to have serious doubts about this assumption," he said.
"They (the Russians) must realize that the West's car and electronics industries could live with $250 to $300 an ounce palladium for a few years before major substitution or thrifting was seen."

A strike overnight at South Africa's Impala Platinum Ltd was also adding to supply concerns, even though management said production was expected to run close to normal levels "in the short to medium term".
South Africa and Russia are the world's main suppliers of platinum and palladium.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
